method: Read both digest.md files, desktop-fold.png, sheet-desktop.png, mobile-fold.png and sheet-mobile.png for ref-0011 and ref-0012 (8 tool calls). Not verified: live pages, product pages, cart/checkout, real prices beyond the homepage, review authenticity, the Allure award, the 'clinically tested' and 'patented' claims, the expert's identity, the third-party test reports, and whether the ERLY 10% pop-up really reopens on scroll or only did so in the capture. Star ratings are not in the text layer (only 'out 5 stars'), so the score itself was not read. No eye tracking: statements about where the eye goes are inferred from layout.

ref-0011.business: ERLY: dermatologist-founded, fragrance-free DTC skincare (Shopify). The action that pays is a first order of a cleanser/serum/moisturizer routine; the secondary action is the email+SMS sign-up for 10% off.

reasons.business: Trust before the ask is good: 'Derm-Developed. Clinically Tested.' bar, Allure Best of Beauty 2026 badge on the fold. But the homepage shows no product prices (the only prices, $16 and $22, are cart-drawer upsells for a claw clip and a brush), no reviews or ratings (proof words: none), and every main CTA is soft ('DISCOVER ERLY', 'EXPLORE SERUMS', 'DISCOVER YOUR ROUTINE'). The strongest ask on the page is the 10% email pop-up, not a product.
reasons.customer: Phone visitor's questions in order: what is this and is it for my skin, does it work, what does it cost, which one do I start with, can I trust it. The fold answers 'award-winning product' but not what ERLY is (no H1; the hero headline is 'Allure Best of Beauty Winner, Daily Splash'). 'Fragrance-free' and 'all skin types' exist only in the meta description. Step 1-2-3 routine answers 'where do I start' well. Price and reviews are unanswered on the homepage. Mobile fold itself is clean (no overlay, CTA visible), but 27 tap targets under 24px and the sheets show the 10% pop-up covering every later screen.
reasons.story: One message holds: 'Good skin starts with keeping it simple' -> a 3-step routine -> 'real skin, things that have lived a little' -> morning (SPF) and all-day glow (Daily Dew). Each section earns the next. Weakened by the missing title: the fold sells one award, the brand thesis only arrives in the second section.

claims.evidence: Few sections (8 headings, steps 1-3, two product features) and a clear order, so the reading path is simple. The system is not: 3 full-screen sticky panels, 4 typefaces, 8 background colours (#47c3ca, #fadb95, #1acc5d, #ffa5a7 ...), radii 9999/12/26/24px, and a sticky 31%-of-screen cart drawer. Simple to read, not simple in construction.

claims.claim: It works because of good photo choices.
claims.verdict: Half true: the photos carry the brand, not the sale
claims.evidence: Sun-lit outdoor portraits with the product held to the face (fold) and the 'real skin' editorial give the brand its character. 'Works' as a shop is not shown: no prices, no reviews, no H1, soft CTAs. The photos make it memorable; nothing on the page makes it convert beyond the 10% pop-up.

claims.claim: The typography is very minimal: big images, small text, big space.
claims.evidence: Four typefaces (Build 61%, Signifier serif 31%, plus fallbacks). The key copy is not small: on mobile 'Good skin starts with keeping it simple...' is a large serif paragraph mixed with bold sans and coloured dots, and the footer has a giant ERLY logotype. Big images and generous space are true; 'small text' and 'minimal' are not.

claims.claim: The images carry it, so the eye moves to the photos.
claims.verdict: Plausible for the fold, not measured
claims.evidence: Desktop and mobile folds are a full-bleed photo with no H1; the red Allure badge and the yellow pill are the next highest-contrast stops, so the badge competes with the face. No eye-tracking data; inferred from composition only.

problems: No prices or ratings on the homepage: the visitor cannot judge value or social proof without leaving the page.
No H1 / no brand statement on the fold: the hero names an award for one product, not what ERLY is or who it is for ('fragrance-free, all skin types' lives only in the meta description).

Interruptions: the 10% pop-up appears over every captured scroll screen and a cart-drawer upsell (claw clip, brush) is sticky at 31% of screen height; 8 text items never become visible (also under reduced motion).
keep: Numbered 3-step routine (Cleanse -> Serum -> Moisturizer) with one CTA per step: turns a catalogue into a starting path for a beginner.
Third-party award badge on the hero photo: borrowed trust placed before any ask.
Thin trust bar above the nav ('Derm-Developed. Clinically Tested.'): two credentials read before the logo.
Ingredient call-outs on product features (Zinc Oxide SPF 40; Ploretin, Niacinamide): a fast 'what is in it' answer next to the product.

ref-0012.business: Sunny Within: DTC liposomal supplements in single-serve gel pouches (Shopify). The action that pays is a subscription (regular vs subscription price on every card, free gift with first subscription); secondary actions are the quiz and the 20%-off email sign-up.

reasons.business: Offer, price and ask are explicit: six product cards each with category, review count, one-line benefit, regular and subscription price ($79/$63 etc.) and ADD TO CART; 'FREE GIFT WITH YOUR FIRST SUBSCRIPTION' bar; 'Subscribe & Save' and quiz in the nav. Trust is stacked before the second ask: review counts (up to 1042), 8 attribute badges incl. 3rd-party tested, a named MD testimonial, a footer link to third-party tests, and an FDA disclaimer plus one cited study. Held back by the primary CTA itself: white text on the orange gradient measures 2.3:1 on mobile, and review counts are set at 8px.
reasons.customer: Phone visitor's questions: what is it, will it help me, what's in it, what does it cost, does it really work, is it safe. Answered in roughly that order: H1 immunity, ingredients on the hero pouch and the cards, price on the cards, review counts, 'how liposomal works', expert, third-party tests. Mobile costs: the cookie banner covers half the first screen, body text is 9-14px, 40 tap targets under 24px, 104 text items within 12px of the edge, and the star score itself is not in the text layer.
reasons.story: Sections earn their place (product -> why liposomal -> bestseller -> expert -> reasons -> sign-up), but there are two messages: the hero sells seasonal immunity, while the rest of the page is built around longevity ('Better on a cellular level', 'The ultimate longevity blend', 'Help your cells age brilliantly', the longevity expert). Longevity is pitched twice, with near-identical bullets.

claims.claim: The layout is better than ERLY's.
claims.evidence: The brief asks to judge each site against its own business, not rank them. Reframed: as a shop, Sunny Within's homepage answers more buying questions (price, reviews, ingredients, subscription). As a visual system it is busier, not cleaner: 13 font sizes, 10 radius values, 21 gradients, 53 endless animation loops with no pause control.

claims.claim: It feels modern because of a large, consistent corner radius.
claims.evidence: Measured radii: 40, 10, 55, 44, 8, 2.5, 87, 30px, 50% and 999px, i.e. ten values. Large rounding (pill buttons, ~40px panels, the rounded hero bottom corner) is visible and contributes to the soft DTC feel, but 'modern' also comes from the gradients, the olive/lime palette and the serif-plus-italic headline pairing.

claims.claim: The images support it; without them it would look old.
claims.evidence: No image-free render was captured. The photography (pouch with orange, macro gel, smiling model) does much of the appetite work. Without it, the Herbik serif with italic and the cream/olive panels would read as classic-editorial; the pill buttons, card grid and gradients would still read as current DTC. 'Old' is not supported by the evidence either way.

claims.claim: Colour play is good, consistent, and makes a brand rather than just a website.
claims.evidence: Olive #373c00 / cream #fffaf0 / lime #e6ef8e / orange #fc6125 recur in the top bar, logo, CTAs, testimonial panel and footer wordmark, so the palette reads as a brand. Exceptions: per-product category tags add pink/purple/blue gradients (inspector flags 3 purple gradients, 7 chromatic colours on mobile), and 25-27 text elements fail WCAG AA, including the main SHOP NOW.

problems: Two competing messages: a seasonal immunity hero on top of a page that is mostly about longevity, so the first promise and the main story differ.

Health copy goes further than its sources: 'Play good defense this sick season' implies preventing illness that the FDA disclaimer disowns; 'Liposomal delivery gets nutrients directly to your cells' has no asterisk or source; 'patented technology', 'first complete NAD+ pathway formula' and 'replaces 7+ supplements' are unsourced on the page.
Phone legibility and access: cookie banner over half the first screen, 8-10px text on reviews and the expert credit, the primary orange CTA at about 2.3:1 contrast, 40 small tap targets.
keep: Product card with regular and subscription price side by side plus direct ADD TO CART: shows the saving and removes a click.
Category label + review count + one-line benefit with key ingredients on each card: answers 'for what, does it work, what's in it' in one glance.
Attribute badge strip (vegan, gluten-free, 3rd-party tested, sugar-free): objection handling in one scrollable line.
Footer compliance block with a named study citation and a 'Third-Party Tests' link: claims can be traced, which is the right pattern for supplements.
Product photographed with its key ingredient (pouch with orange): shows the format and the flavour at once.
ref-0012.veto: Unsourced health claims presented as fact in the copy, not the design: the hero frames an immunity supplement as defence for 'sick season' (implied illness prevention, contradicted by the site's own 'not intended to prevent any disease' disclaimer), and 'Liposomal delivery gets nutrients directly to your cells' carries no asterisk or source. Keep the layout patterns; do not copy the claims.
